p01-closeness-title.name: p01-closeness-title
p01-closeness-title.text: When classes overlap and cannot be separated, ask instead: how close can the output get to the target ±1?

p01-closeness-ctx.name: p01-closeness-ctx
p01-closeness-ctx.text: A 1-D feature $x$. The target is $y=+1$ (positive) or $-1$ (negative). Use a line through the origin $\widehat y=w\,x$ to approximate these targets.

p01-closeness-src.name: p01-closeness-src
p01-closeness-src.text: Source: KP07 lecture §1; the 6 points are this page's teaching data (negative $-1.5,-0.8,0.2$, positive $-0.2,0.9,1.6$). The lecture's $J$ is an expectation; here it is replaced by the mean of 6 data points.

p01-closeness-c0.name: p01-closeness-c0
p01-closeness-c0.text: Blue circles (positive) and red triangles (negative) overlap on the $x$ axis: the negative at $0.2$ is further right than the positive at $-0.2$. Can one threshold separate them completely?

p01-closeness-c1.name: p01-closeness-c1
p01-closeness-c1.text: The green line $\widehat y=w\,x$ is the one closest to all targets: $w=0.694$ (details on the next page).

p01-closeness-c2.name: p01-closeness-c2
p01-closeness-c2.text: The vertical distances from the three positive points to the line (orange dashed): the residual $e=y-\widehat y$.

p01-closeness-c3.name: p01-closeness-c3
p01-closeness-c3.text: Residuals of the three negative points. Mean squared error $J=\dfrac16\sum e_i^2=0.491$, not 0.

p01-closeness-c4.name: p01-closeness-c4
p01-closeness-c4.text: Learning compares the continuous output with $\pm1$; classification looks at the sign of $\widehat y$ only at the end. This line misclassifies the two points $x=0.2$, $x=-0.2$, yet it is still the line with the smallest $J$.

p02-bowl-title.name: p02-bowl-title
p02-bowl-title.text: Why w≈0.694? Plot J against w: it is a bowl; the slope at the bottom is 0

p02-bowl-ctx.name: p02-bowl-ctx
p02-bowl-ctx.text: $J(w)=E[y^2]-2w\,p+w^2R$, where $R=E[x^2]$ and $p=E[xy]$. The previous page's data: $E[y^2]=1$, $R=1.057$, $p=0.733$.

p02-bowl-src.name: p02-bowl-src
p02-bowl-src.text: Source: KP07 lecture §2: $\nabla J=-2\mathbf p+2R_x\mathbf w$, correcting the source's $+2E[\mathbf xe]$ (the gradient descent direction must be right). This page uses a scalar weight; $R,p$ come from the 6 data points.

p02-bowl-c0.name: p02-bowl-c0
p02-bowl-c0.text: $J$ is a quadratic function of $w$; its graph is a bowl. Where is the lowest point? What is the slope there?

p02-bowl-c1.name: p02-bowl-c1
p02-bowl-c1.text: Blue is $J(w)$. As long as $R>0$ it opens upward and has a unique lowest point.

p02-bowl-c2.name: p02-bowl-c2
p02-bowl-c2.text: At $w=0$: the slope (gradient) $=-2p+2Rw=-1.467<0$ (the orange line slopes down). To reduce $J$, $w$ should go right (increase), so the update is $w\leftarrow w-\eta\nabla J=w+2\eta\,E[x\,e]$.

p02-bowl-c3.name: p02-bowl-c3
p02-bowl-c3.text: Lowest point: slope $=0$, i.e. $Rw=p$, so $w^{\ast}=p/R=0.694$, $J_{\min}=0.491$. This is the normal equation.

p02-bowl-c4.name: p02-bowl-c4
p02-bowl-c4.text: The vector case is the same: $\nabla J=-2\mathbf p+2R_x\mathbf w=0\Rightarrow R_x\mathbf w=\mathbf p$. The gradient has a minus sign (because the residual is defined as $y-\mathbf x^T\mathbf w$).

p03-expand-title.name: p03-expand-title
p03-expand-title.text: J is really a sum of three terms: a constant, a line and a parabola

p03-expand-ctx.name: p03-expand-ctx
p03-expand-ctx.text: Expand $J(w)=E[(y-xw)^2]=E[y^2]-2p\,w+R\,w^2$: a constant, a line and a parabola, each in a small plot.

p03-expand-src.name: p03-expand-src
p03-expand-src.text: Source: KP07 lecture §2 expansion; the three terms use the previous page's data ($E[y^2]=1$, $p=0.733$, $R=1.057$), computed by build_kp07_en.py.

p03-expand-c0.name: p03-expand-c0
p03-expand-c0.text: What does each of the three parts of $J$ look like? What do we get adding them up? See the first plot first.

p03-expand-c1.name: p03-expand-c1
p03-expand-c1.text: Term 1 $E[y^2]=1$: the targets are all $\pm1$, so their squares are all 1 and the average is a constant independent of $w$.

p03-expand-c2.name: p03-expand-c2
p03-expand-c2.text: Term 2 $-2pw=-1.467\,w$: $p=E[xy]$ is the correlation of feature and target. The slope is negative, so this term decreases as $w$ grows.

p03-expand-c3.name: p03-expand-c3
p03-expand-c3.text: Term 3 $Rw^2$: $R=E[x^2]=1.057>0$, so it is an upward parabola; the penalty grows when $w$ is too large.

p03-expand-c4.name: p03-expand-c4
p03-expand-c4.text: Adding the three: constant + falling line + rising parabola = a bowl. The bottom is where the two forces balance: $-2p+2Rw=0$.

p04-orthogonal-title.name: p04-orthogonal-title
p04-orthogonal-title.text: In 3-D: the best prediction is a projection; the residual is perpendicular to the plane of all usable directions

p04-orthogonal-ctx.name: p04-orthogonal-ctx
p04-orthogonal-ctx.text: A vector example: two bases $\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2$ lie in the plane $z=0$; the target $\mathbf y$ is above the plane. A prediction can only land inside the plane.

p04-orthogonal-src.name: p04-orthogonal-src
p04-orthogonal-src.text: Source: KP07 lecture §3–§4 3-D example; $\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2,\mathbf y$ follow the lecture's initial values. Note: the two columns of $X$ are bases, not two feature coordinates of a single sample.

p04-orthogonal-c0.name: p04-orthogonal-c0
p04-orthogonal-c0.text: $\widehat{\mathbf y}$ can only be a linear combination of $\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2$, i.e. lie in the gray plane. The target $\mathbf y$ is off the plane. Where is the point in the plane nearest to $\mathbf y$?

p04-orthogonal-c1.name: p04-orthogonal-c1
p04-orthogonal-c1.text: The red arrow is the target $\mathbf y=(1.35,0.85,1.25)$. Its third component is not 0, so it is not in the plane.

p04-orthogonal-c2.name: p04-orthogonal-c2
p04-orthogonal-c2.text: Dropping straight down from $\mathbf y$ to the plane, the landing point is the projection $\widehat{\mathbf y}=(1.35,0.85,0)$; the orange dashed line is the residual $\mathbf e=\mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y}=(0,0,1.25)$.

p04-orthogonal-c3.name: p04-orthogonal-c3
p04-orthogonal-c3.text: The residual is perpendicular to both bases: $\mathbf e^T\mathbf b_1=0$, $\mathbf e^T\mathbf b_2=0$. Perpendicular to both bases means perpendicular to any linear combination of them (the whole plane).

p04-orthogonal-c4.name: p04-orthogonal-c4
p04-orthogonal-c4.text: This is the geometric meaning of "zero gradient": $E[x_j e]=0$, the residual is orthogonal to every feature direction.

p05-coeff-title.name: p05-coeff-title
p05-coeff-title.text: Compute the projection's coefficients: solve the 2×2 normal equation

p05-coeff-ctx.name: p05-coeff-ctx
p05-coeff-ctx.text: $\widehat{\mathbf y}=X\mathbf w$, $X=[\mathbf b_1\;\mathbf b_2]$. Normal equation $X^TX\,\mathbf w=X^T\mathbf y$. (Here $\mathbf w$ is 2 coefficients, while $\mathbf y,\widehat{\mathbf y}$ are 3-D vectors.)

p05-coeff-src.name: p05-coeff-src
p05-coeff-src.text: Source: KP07 lecture §4 numbers: $X^TX$, $X^T\mathbf y$, $\widehat{\mathbf w}\approx(0.8592523,0.9814955)$; recomputed by build_kp07_en.py and independently by check_numbers_kp07.py.

p05-coeff-c0.name: p05-coeff-c0
p05-coeff-c0.text: First compute the two matrices $X^TX$ and $X^T\mathbf y$. Then solve for the two coefficients and finally combine them into $\widehat{\mathbf y}$.

p05-coeff-c2.name: p05-coeff-c2
p05-coeff-c2.text: Solving gives $\widehat{\mathbf w}=(0.8592523,\;0.9814955)$: go $0.859$ along $\mathbf b_1$ and $0.981$ along $\mathbf b_2$.

p05-coeff-c3.name: p05-coeff-c3
p05-coeff-c3.text: Head to tail: $0.859\,\mathbf b_1+0.981\,\mathbf b_2=(1.35,0.85,0)=\widehat{\mathbf y}$. Consistent with the green point on the previous page.

p05-coeff-c4.name: p05-coeff-c4
p05-coeff-c4.text: Residual $\mathbf e=\mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y}=(0,0,1.25)$, $\|\mathbf e\|^2=1.25^2=1.5625$. The coefficients are 2-D, the projection point is 3-D; do not mix them up.

p06-pythagoras-title.name: p06-pythagoras-title
p06-pythagoras-title.text: Why is the projection nearest? Any other point in the plane only makes the error larger

p06-pythagoras-ctx.name: p06-pythagoras-ctx
p06-pythagoras-ctx.text: Compare $\widehat{\mathbf y}$ with another in-plane prediction $\tilde{\mathbf y}=(1,1,0)$: the squared distance to the target $\mathbf y$ is the sum of two parts.

p06-pythagoras-src.name: p06-pythagoras-src
p06-pythagoras-src.text: Source: KP07 lecture §3 Pythagorean relation $E[(y-\tilde y)^2]=E[(y-\hat y)^2]+E[(\hat y-\tilde y)^2]$; $\tilde{\mathbf y}=(1,1,0)$ is another in-plane point chosen for this page.

p06-pythagoras-c0.name: p06-pythagoras-c0
p06-pythagoras-c0.text: The green point $\widehat{\mathbf y}$ (projection) and the purple point $\tilde{\mathbf y}$ (another prediction) are both in the plane. Which is nearer to the red point $\mathbf y$? How are their distances related?

p06-pythagoras-c1.name: p06-pythagoras-c1
p06-pythagoras-c1.text: Orange: $\|\mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y}\|^2=1.5625$ (the residual, perpendicular to the plane).

p06-pythagoras-c3.name: p06-pythagoras-c3
p06-pythagoras-c3.text: The squared distance from $\tilde{\mathbf y}$ to $\mathbf y$ is $1.7075$ = $1.5625+0.145$. The two sides are perpendicular, so it is a right triangle and the hypotenuse is longest.

p06-pythagoras-c4.name: p06-pythagoras-c4
p06-pythagoras-c4.text: The second term $\|\widehat{\mathbf y}-\tilde{\mathbf y}\|^2\ge0$ (the cross term vanishes by perpendicularity), so any other in-plane point only adds error: the projection is the minimum.

p07-caveats-title.name: p07-caveats-title
p07-caveats-title.text: The best projection does not mean no error, nor the fewest misclassifications: outliers can pull the line askew

p07-caveats-ctx.name: p07-caveats-ctx
p07-caveats-ctx.text: Back to page 1's 1-D data. Add one point far to the right with target $+1$ too, $x=8$: it is also "correct", but what happens to the best line?

p07-caveats-src.name: p07-caveats-src
p07-caveats-src.text: Source: KP07 lecture §5 "common myths" (squared error is sensitive to extremes; best projection ≠ lowest misclassification rate); the $x=8$ point is a teaching contrast added on this page, numbers computed by build_kp07_en.py.

p07-caveats-c0.name: p07-caveats-c0
p07-caveats-c0.text: The green line is the original line closest to the six points (slope $0.694$). After adding the $x=8$ point, does the best line get steeper or flatter?

p07-caveats-c1.name: p07-caveats-c1
p07-caveats-c1.text: The new point $(8,+1)$: far from the others, its target differs greatly from the old line's output $5.55$.

p07-caveats-c2.name: p07-caveats-c2
p07-caveats-c2.text: Re-fitting the best: the slope falls from $0.694$ to $0.176$ (orange line, much flatter). One far point pulls the whole line askew.

p07-caveats-c3.name: p07-caveats-c3
p07-caveats-c3.text: The old line's mean squared error on the new data is $3.381$; the re-fitted best is $0.688$. Squared error squares and amplifies large residuals, so it cares especially about outliers.

p07-caveats-c4.name: p07-caveats-c4
p07-caveats-c4.text: So: the best projection does not guarantee zero residual or the fewest errors; squared error also needs a finite second moment. For multiple outputs the targets are one-hot, and $E\|\mathbf y-W^T\mathbf x\|^2$ splits into $M$ scalar problems.

p08-practice-title.name: p08-practice-title
p08-practice-title.text: Practice: bases (1,0,0), (0,1,0), target (2,−1,3): find the coefficients, projection and residual

p08-practice-ctx.name: p08-practice-ctx
p08-practice-ctx.text: Work it out first: write the two columns of $X$, solve the normal equation and finally check the residual's inner products with the two bases. Press Next when done.

p08-practice-src.name: p08-practice-src
p08-practice-src.text: Source: KP07 lecture practice; answer computed by build_kp07_en.py and recomputed independently by check_numbers_kp07.py.

p08-practice-q.name: p08-practice-q
p08-practice-q.text: (a) The coefficients $\widehat{\mathbf w}$? (b) The projection $\widehat{\mathbf y}$? (c) The residual $\mathbf e$, its inner products with the two bases, and $\|\mathbf e\|^2$?

p08-practice-a1.name: p08-practice-a1
p08-practice-a1.text: (a) $X^TX=I$, $X^T\mathbf y=(2,-1)^T$, so $\widehat{\mathbf w}=(2,-1)$. (b) $\widehat{\mathbf y}=(2,-1,0)$ (green point: drop the third component).

p08-practice-a2.name: p08-practice-a2
p08-practice-a2.text: (c) $\mathbf e=\mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y}=(0,0,3)$ (orange dashed); $\mathbf e^T\mathbf b_1=\mathbf e^T\mathbf b_2=0$; $\|\mathbf e\|^2=3^2=9$.

p08-practice-a3.name: p08-practice-a3
p08-practice-a3.text: This time the bases are perpendicular, $X^TX$ is the identity, and the coefficients are just the target's coordinates on the two axes. The earlier example had an angle between the bases, which is why a $2\times2$ solve was needed.

p09-summary-title.name: p09-summary-title
p09-summary-title.text: Summary: J is a bowl, the lowest point has slope 0, the prediction is a projection, the residual is perpendicular

p09-summary-ctx.name: p09-summary-ctx
p09-summary-ctx.text: Recall along the 3-D example; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p09-summary-e0.name: p09-summary-e0
p09-summary-e0.text: When data overlap we ask "how close": $J=E[(y-\mathbf x^T\mathbf w)^2]$, and look at the sign only at the end for classification

p09-summary-e1.name: p09-summary-e1
p09-summary-e1.text: $J=E[y^2]-2\mathbf w^T\mathbf p+\mathbf w^TR\mathbf w$, $\nabla J=-2\mathbf p+2R\mathbf w$; setting $\nabla J=0$ gives $R\mathbf w=\mathbf p$

p09-summary-e2.name: p09-summary-e2
p09-summary-e2.text: The best prediction is a projection: the residual is orthogonal to every feature direction, $E[x_je]=0$

p09-summary-e3.name: p09-summary-e3
p09-summary-e3.text: The projection is nearest (Pythagoras); but the residual is not 0 and misclassifications are not necessarily fewest; squared error is sensitive to outliers

p09-summary-e4.name: p09-summary-e4
p09-summary-e4.text: Open question: with no distribution and data arriving one at a time, how do we approach this optimum? Next KP: LMS
